subject: Uniform sampling from a convex polytope

messages.author: 1356bff10164b43d
messages.subject: Uniform sampling from a convex polytope
parts:
Hi, I am a new user to Stan. It seems to me that Stan excels in MCMC sampling, so I wonder if it will be possible for me to use Stan to sample uniformly from the solution space of Ax = b, where A is a coefficient matrix and b is a single-column matrix of constants. Currently, I have a R package which implements hit-and-run algorithm to do the sampling, but the convergence is slow and the mixing is not satisfactory. Referred below is the link to a posted last year which seems highly relevant to my question:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/sampling$20simplex/stan-users/jYWbXdHAa4k/w0VJAMuYGtUJ

Thanks in advance for any response!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Uniform sampling from a convex polytope
parts:
If you can write down an expression proportional to a
proper log posterior, then Stan should be able to sample
from it (with some caveats about posterior curvature).

It may seem like this model would work:

data {
int<lower=1> K;
vector[K] b;
}
parameters {
matrix[K] A;
}
transformed parameters {
vector[K] x;
x <- A \ b;
}
model {
}

The way this works, though, is that an empty model means a
uniform distribution on the parameters. So that would be
uniform in A, which is improper (uniforms are only proper on
finite-volume subsets).

To make it uniform in x, you need to add the log Jacobian
determinant of the transform from A to x into the model:

increment_log_prob(log_det_J);

I'm not good enough at linear algebra to tell you what that
is without spending all day on it, and I'm also not sure offhand
if the posterior will be proper.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Uniform sampling from a convex polytope
parts:
It's not clear what the actual model is -- are you trying to sample x or A? 

The posterior for x will be atrocious unless you add some regularization.  

Given the subject title, perhaps you're sampling form A and the columns of A sum to 1? In that case you just create a bunch of simplices, assign the columns to A, and go.  You should also put Dirichlet priors on the simplices to clean everything up.

parts:
Without any prior, the default is uniform on the simplex,
i.e., Dirichlet(1). If you want more regularization, you'll
need to include a Dirichlet prior directly.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Uniform sampling from a convex polytope
parts:
Thanks for the reply Mike! 

A more exact formulation of my question will be: sample x uniformly, given that Ax = b and x > = 0, and x is not unbounded. For example, in the three dimensional case, if A is a 2 by 3 matrix whose first row is c(1, 1, 1) and whose second row is c(1, 0, 0) and b is c(1, 0.5), then I would like to sample some (x1, x2, x3) uniformly from {(x1, x2, x3) | x1 = 0.5, x2 + x3 = 0.5}. Of course, I want to know if there is a general solution for higher dimensions in Stan. Solving this linear sampling question is very meaningful in that it has many direct applications in other problems which involve such randomization and it will be great if Stan is able to do this.

Yuanchu

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Uniform sampling from a convex polytope
parts:
On Wednesday, July 23, 2014 3:58:24 PM UTC-4, Yuanchu Dang wrote:
I think I forgot to point out that I would like to sample from only the positive solution space of Ax = b. For example, if A is a 1 by 3 matrix whose entries are all 1 and b is 1, then I want to sample uniformly from the triangle connecting (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1). Of course, A may have more than one one row and so may b. Moreover, I will make sure that the input I supply has a finite measure. Do you know how to add that constraint of positivity?

It is easy to specify that all elements of a parameter vector must be positive

parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[K] x;
}

but I think it would be hard for Stan to sample uniformally from the sample space of x. If the model block is simply a binary question of whether x is or is not admissible, I have difficulty seeing how NUTS could perform much better than hit-and-run. It seems like NUTS would basically keep making proposals until it hit the boundary of the sample space and then do a slice sample from among its footprints, which is pretty much what I understand hit-and-run to be doing.

Ben

I will cheat and do it for this particular b and A:

library(rstan)

A <- matrix(1, nrow = 1, ncol = 3)
b <- 1
dim(b) <- 1 # necessary

code <-
'
data {
  int<lower=1> m; // m = 1
  int<lower=1> n; // n = 3
  vector[m] b;
  matrix[m,n] A;
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> x_1;
  real<lower=0,upper=(b[1] - A[1,1] * x_1)> x_2;
  real<lower=0,upper=(b[1] - A[1,1] * x_1 - A[1,2] * x_2)> x_3;
}
model {

}
'

d <- list(m = 1, n = 3, b = b, A = A)
fit <- stan(model_code = code, data = d)
pairs(fit) # triangles

Doing it for arbitrary b and A would be very tedious in Stan. But, moreover, I don't think NUTS is of much help when there is an empty model block since the partial derivatives are zero everywhere.

Ben

parts:
On Thursday, July 24, 2014 1:15:15 PM UTC-4, Yuanchu Dang wrote:
Thanks, Ben, for your code! 

I can see now that doing my sampling with Stan may be tedious... and using only upper or lower bound in the bracket may not be a reproducible way for A with multiple rows. Another concern will be that (in this particular case) it seems that Stan will first sample x1 from [0, 1], then sample x2 from [0, 1 - x2] and then x3 from [0, 1 - x1 - x2]. But mathematically this will produce a different distribution than the uniform triangle of (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1).

Using the notation from

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_linear_equations#Matrix_solution

here is how it could (in principle) be done generically

library(rstan)
library(MASS)

A <- matrix(1, nrow = 1, ncol = 3)
b <- 1
dim(b) <- 1

Ag <- ginv(A)

code <-
  '

data {
  int<lower=1> m;
  int<lower=1> n;
  vector[m] b;
  matrix[m,n] A;

matrix[n,m] Ag;
}
transformed data {
  matrix[n,n] ImAgA;
  vector[n] Agb;
  Agb <- Ag * b;
  ImAgA <- -Ag*A;
  for(i in 1:n) ImAgA[i,i] <- ImAgA[i,i] + 1.0;

Stan spits out one such "Informational Message" every time the positivity constraint on x is violated and piping all that text through to RStudio results in a lot of overhead that is not counted in the Elapsed Time. It seems to be tolerable when I use R from a shell. Alternatively, you could use parLapply() in the parallel library to start a background R process (or processes to do the chains in parallel), in which case I think all that "Informational Message" text would get diverted somewhere.
